lessons.title: Budgeting vs Cash Forecasting: Why You Need Both

children.text: Most Indian companies of any size build an annual budget. Far fewer build a cash forecast, and many managers assume the budget already is one. It is not. A budget answers whether the year will be profitable. A cash forecast answers whether the business can pay everyone on the 7th, the 15th and the 20th of next month. Both are necessary, they are built differently, and the gap between them is where September goes wrong.

body.text: A budget is a promise about profit for the year. A cash forecast is a prediction about the bank balance on a particular date. You can deliver the first perfectly and still fail the second.

columns.label: Budget
points: Built on accruals: revenue when billed, costs when incurred
Usually annual, split by month and by department
Owned by department heads and measured as variance against plan
Includes depreciation, excludes loan principal and capex payments
Answers: will we make our profit target?

columns.label: Cash forecast
points: Built on dates: money in and out of the bank
Usually weekly for the near term, monthly beyond it, and rolled forward constantly
Owned by finance, but fed by sales, procurement and HR
Excludes depreciation, includes every EMI, capex cheque and tax payment
Answers: will we have money in the bank that week?

body.text: The most common failure in Indian SMEs is not a missing budget. It is a budget with no cash translation, presented monthly to people who quite reasonably conclude that because every department is on plan, the company is fine.

children.text: Konkan Ceramics budgets ₹1 crore of sales a month, ₹70 lakh of cost of goods sold and ₹20 lakh of overheads, so ₹10 lakh of profit a month and ₹1.2 crore for the year. September is a festive build-up month. The budget says the month went exactly to plan.

body.text: Notice which three lines do the most damage: capex, loan principal and advance tax. All three are invisible in a profit budget, all three are known months in advance, and all three are large. If your company forecasts nothing else, forecast those.

body.title: Build the bridge yourself
body.prompt: Next month's budget shows ₹25 lakh of profit, including ₹8 lakh of depreciation. Receivables are expected to rise by ₹20 lakh and payables by ₹6 lakh, with inventory flat. The company will pay ₹12 lakh for a delivery van and ₹3 lakh of loan principal, with no tax payment due. What is the expected movement in the bank balance, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: 25 plus 8 for depreciation is 33. Subtract 20 for higher receivables and add 6 for higher payables, giving 19. Subtract 12 for the van and 3 for loan principal, leaving ₹4 lakh. A month budgeted at ₹25 lakh of profit adds ₹4 lakh to the bank, and that is a good month, not a bad one.

children.text: Profit Is Smooth, Cash Is Not
Plot the two side by side across the festive half-year and the point becomes obvious. Budgeted profit is a steady ₹10 lakh a month. The bank balance goes on a journey.

body.title: Konkan Ceramics: cumulative budgeted profit vs bank balance (₹ lakh)

children.text: Across the six months the business earns ₹60 lakh of profit and adds ₹14 lakh to the bank, which is a perfectly healthy outcome. But it needs an overdraft of at least ₹43 lakh at the end of September to get there. A budget alone will never tell you that number, and the bank will want to hear it before September, not during it.

body.title: Direct and indirect forecasting, and when to use each

children.text: There are two ways to build a cash forecast, and mature finance teams run both.

List expected receipts and payments by date: this customer pays on the 12th, wages on the 1st, GST on the 20th. Accurate for the next 6 to 13 weeks, and useless beyond a quarter because you cannot name the invoices yet.

Start from the budgeted profit and bridge it to cash, exactly as in the table above. Less precise week to week, but the only workable approach for 6 to 18 months ahead, and it plugs straight into the annual budget.

The practical split used by most well-run companies: a direct 13-week forecast updated weekly for operational decisions, which Lesson 4.2 builds step by step, and an indirect annual forecast refreshed each quarter for funding decisions, limit renewals and capex approvals.

One habit matters more than the method: roll it forward. A forecast built in April and never updated is a historical document by June. Reforecast monthly, and compare each week's actual bank balance against what you predicted, so the errors teach you something.

Budgets have owners by design: every line has a department head who answers for it. Cash usually has only one owner, finance, which is why it is forecast badly. Most of the information finance needs sits with other people.

cells: Which customers will genuinely pay this month, and who is disputing an invoice
A weekly collections call-over by customer, not a total
When large orders will be placed and what terms were agreed
Committed purchase orders with expected payment dates
When the festive build-up starts and how much stock it needs
The build-up plan in rupees, by month
Joining dates, increments, bonus timing, full and final settlements
The payroll number by month, including statutory dues and their due dates
When a machine will be delivered and the payment milestone falls
Capex payment dates, not approval dates

body.text: This is the practical reason cash forecasting fails in companies that are otherwise well run. The forecast is only as good as the five conversations behind it, and each of those five people is measured on something other than cash.

body.title: In the budget, but not in the bank
body.question: Which of these appears in a monthly profit budget but has no effect on the bank balance that month?
options: The advance tax instalment paid on 15 September
The principal portion of a term loan EMI
A supplier invoice paid on the day it was received
body.explanation: Depreciation is a budgeted cost with no cash movement. Advance tax and the supplier payment are cash movements that a profit budget shows in a different period or in a different form. Loan principal is the reverse of depreciation: real cash, entirely absent from the budget.

body.title: Which forecast for which horizon
body.textWithBlank: A short-term forecast listing expected receipts and payments by date uses the ___ method.
body.explanation: The direct method works from actual expected bank movements and is accurate for about 6 to 13 weeks. The indirect method starts from budgeted profit and bridges to cash, which is what you need for horizons beyond a quarter.

body.title: But it is in the budget
body.scenario: It is 2 September. The marketing head has approval for a ₹25 lakh festive campaign, which is in the approved annual budget and was signed off by the board in April. The agency wants 100% payment in advance before it books media. Your cash forecast shows the bank balance going to minus ₹43 lakh by the end of September, against a sanctioned overdraft limit of ₹40 lakh. The marketing head's position is simple: the money is budgeted, and the campaign drives the festive quarter.
body.prompt: How do you handle this without either breaching the limit or killing the festive quarter?
body.modelAnswer:
Separate the two questions.
1. Being in the budget means the company agreed to the cost. It says nothing about whether the cash exists in the week the agency wants it. Both statements can be true: the campaign is affordable for the year and unpayable on 5 September.
2. Establish the hard constraint. At minus ₹43 lakh against a ₹40 lakh limit, the account will bounce. A returned payment or a dishonoured cheque damages the banking relationship far more than a delayed campaign.
Then find the timing solutions, in order of preference.
3. Split the payment. Offer 40% now and 60% on 5 October, when collections from festive billing start arriving. Most agencies will take a firm dated commitment over a lost booking.
4. Move the controllable outflows out of the same fortnight. The ₹15 lakh machine payment is the obvious candidate: ask for delivery after 10 October, or milestone-linked payment.
5. Accelerate an inflow. The ₹25 lakh of receivables beyond 60 days from Lesson 3.1 is worth a focused two-week collection push, and bill discounting on accepted invoices can bring in cash within days.
6. Talk to the bank before you need to, not after. A temporary limit enhancement requested in the first week of September with a credible forecast is a routine conversation. The same request on 28 September, after a bounce, is not.
Then fix the process.
7. The real failure is that a ₹25 lakh advance payment in the tightest week of the year was approved in April with no cash date attached. From the next cycle, every budget approval above a threshold should carry an expected payment month, so finance can lay them against the forecast.
8. Tell the marketing head exactly this, with the forecast in front of both of you. The answer is not no, it is not in that week.

body.title: Turn your budget into a cash forecast
steps: Start with budgeted monthly profit for each of the next twelve months.
Add back depreciation and any other non-cash charges.
Adjust each month for expected movements in receivables, inventory and payables, using your own days from Lesson 2.2.
Subtract capital expenditure in the month it will actually be paid, not the month it was approved.
Subtract loan principal repayments from the sanction letter or repayment schedule.
Subtract tax payments on their statutory dates, including advance tax on 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March.
Add any expected inflows that never appear in a profit budget: a new loan, promoter capital, a security deposit refund.
Run the resulting balance month by month and mark the lowest point, then compare it against your sanctioned limits.
Re-run the whole thing every month with actuals replacing forecasts, and check last month's prediction against what really happened.

cards.definition: An accrual plan of revenue and costs, usually annual, owned by department heads.
A dated prediction of money into and out of the bank, and therefore of the balance.
Built from expected receipts and payments by date. Accurate for roughly 6 to 13 weeks.
Built by bridging budgeted profit to cash. Used for horizons beyond a quarter.
A forecast extended and refreshed every period, so the horizon never shrinks.
The lowest point the forecast bank balance reaches. The number your credit limit must cover.

points: A budget predicts profit on accruals. A cash forecast predicts the bank balance on dates. Neither substitutes for the other.
Konkan Ceramics budgeted ₹10 lakh of profit in September and lost ₹38 lakh of cash, with no budget variance anywhere.
Capex, loan principal and tax payments are large, predictable and completely absent from a profit budget.
Bridge budgeted profit to cash: add back depreciation, adjust working capital, then subtract capex, principal and tax.
Use the direct method for the next 6 to 13 weeks and the indirect method beyond a quarter, and roll both forward every month.
The forecast depends on five people outside finance. Without their dates, it is arithmetic on guesses.

body.text: Konkan Ceramics is fictional and all figures are illustrative. Statutory due dates are simplified and can change. Confirm current requirements with your chartered accountant or finance team.
